criteria.reason: Both feel like realistic e-commerce testing scenarios; B's mid-test peeking pressure matches the prompt's pre-meeting setup slightly better, while A's workplace dialogue sounds more natural than B's didactic replies.

A gives a three-decision arc where the learner actively chooses sample size, chooses whether to run the chance check with AI, and makes the rollout call; B is only two decisions per path and automatically runs the AI p-value check in both decision-1 options.

In A, asking the AI to run the check and show counts is a real decision and colleagues sound natural; in B, both first-step options query the AI automatically and the product manager awkwardly critiques his own preferred choice.

Both give specific, kind, strategy-based notes (and B includes example wording on all improve notes), but A's debrief is much easier for a beginner to read, whereas B's notes and summary use stiff textbook language.
Both get every statistical calculation right, but B stays consistent on every branch whereas A's forward-gap branch mislabels an unchecked full test as lacking enough evidence.
For a beginner case, A introduces hypothesis testing in plain words without upfront notation, whereas B puts p < 0.05 on the opening panel before explaining what a p-value is.

A explains chance checks using concrete frequencies anyone can follow, while B reads like a statistics textbook with phrases like supports a bounded answer and a result at least as extreme as the observed one.

overall.reason: Both outputs are mathematically accurate, but B drops unexplained p < 0.05 notation on the opening panel and uses dense academic prose throughout; A serves a beginner much better with everyday explanations and a three-decision arc that tests all three skills.

criteria.reason: A puts the learner on a real Med-Surg hospital ward with a charge nurse and a Friday supply-order deadline, matching the hospital-ward expectation; B moves the case to a clinic training day reviewing simulation materials with no patient care.

A has three-option choices and two data-bringing time jumps but puts the strong option first on every screen and forces node-1 choices into the same node 2; B varies option order and branches cleanly, but uses telegraphed binary choices, has no time jump, and drops capacity even when skipping the follow-up study.

A's ward colleagues sound like real teammates with lively, distinct voices and let the learner actively consult the AI twice; B's colleagues have clear roles and good AI review habits, but their dialogue feels stiff and didactic.

A's debrief is warmer and includes wording examples on every improve note, but two of its improve notes teach the p-value misconception; B's debrief is completely accurate and specific, even though two improve notes put advice rather than quoted wording in the example field.

B's Fisher's exact test (0.30), sample size estimate (82 per format), and statistical interpretations are all accurate; A gets the numbers right but repeatedly teaches the p-value inversion fallacy (calling p = 0.74 a 74% chance it's pure noise and p = 0.50 a 50% chance of being pure luck).

A pitches concepts at a beginner level with everyday analogies (aside from raw LaTeX in two choices), whereas B introduces Fisher's exact test and uses formal phrasing like planning rates and false-alarm limit.
A uses vivid, everyday language, concrete patient counts, and a coin-toss analogy, and directly practices translating jargon; B reads drier and more formal even in its recommended explanations.

observations.claim: Across three panels, the quality analyst's reply, and two debrief notes, Output A repeatedly teaches the classic p-value inversion fallacy—labeling p-values as Chance of luck (p-value): 74% and 50%, saying {{ai}} showed a 74% chance it's pure noise, and stating A 6-versus-4 split has a 50% chance of being pure luck.
observations.learnerCost: The learner leaves a statistics chapter believing a p-value is the probability that a result is pure luck or noise, a core misconception they will carry into real work.

location.detail: panels (Chance of luck (p-value)), switch-on-1-percent reply and note, and switch-on-80 note

overall.reason: Both outputs have a major issue, so learner cost decides it: B misses the hospital-ward setting by using a clinic training-day simulation and reads drier with binary choices and no time jump, but everything it teaches about hypothesis testing is statistically sound; A is much livelier and more authentic to ward nursing, yet repeatedly teaches a false statistical rule (that a p-value is the probability a result is pure luck or noise) across panels, expert dialogue, and debrief while placing the strong choice first on every screen.
